title: Grade 7 Common Core Math — Answer Key
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>; section is M (main), B1, B2, ... (backward), F1 or F2 (forward)
grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S40-F2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one grade's collection; across collections use uid (for example G5:S40-F2-Q3).
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter, or when the student wrote the text of the correct choice.

Short answer: accept any mathematically equivalent form unless the question asks for a specific form (equivalent fractions, decimals, and mixed numbers; a ratio written as a : b, a to b, or a/b; "x = 5" or "5"; terms of an expression in any order). Units are not required unless the question asks for them.
When an answer has several parts (separated by semicolons, or with labels such as "Rate of change:"), every part must be correct.
Drawing / plotting questions (type plot): correct_answer describes what a correct drawing shows. Judge the student's drawing against it.

Drawing + written questions (type plot_text): the student draws on the figure AND writes an answer. drawing_answer describes the correct drawing and correct_answer the written answer. Both must be correct: every requested point, segment or shape in the drawing, and the written conclusion.

Answer with required work (type work): required_method says what the shown work must use. A correct final answer without that work earns partial credit only; correct work with a slip in the final answer is also partial.
Explain / describe questions: grading_note says what a correct response must include; accept any reasonable wording.
grading_note also lists other accepted answers and the work behind an answer. It is guidance for the grader, not for students.

questions.question: A gym charges $15 to join plus $8 for each class. Max paid $79 in all. (a) Solve with arithmetic. (b) Write and solve an equation. (c) Compare the steps of the two solutions.
questions.required_method: Grade all three parts: (a) a correct arithmetic solution, (b) a correct equation with an algebraic solution, and (c) a comparison that matches each arithmetic operation to the algebra step that does the same thing in the same order. Example: (a) 79 - 15 = 64, 64 ÷ 8 = 8; (b) 8c + 15 = 79, subtract 15 from both sides, then divide both sides by 8; (c) both subtract 15 first and then divide by 8. Any valid equation is accepted.

questions.set_title: Compare an algebraic solution with an arithmetic solution

questions.question: Four friends each buy a ticket and a $3 popcorn. They pay $46 in all. (a) Solve with arithmetic. (b) Write and solve an equation. (c) Compare the steps of the two solutions.
questions.required_method: Grade all three parts: (a) a correct arithmetic solution, (b) a correct equation with an algebraic solution, and (c) a comparison that matches each arithmetic operation to the algebra step that does the same thing in the same order. Example: (a) 46 ÷ 4 = 11.50, 11.50 - 3 = 8.50; (b) 4(t + 3) = 46, divide both sides by 4, then subtract 3; (c) both divide by 4 first and then subtract 3. An equation such as 4t + 12 = 46 is also accepted, with the matching comparison.

questions.section_title: Explain triangle congruence criteria with rigid motions
questions.question: Triangles ABC and DEF have AB = DE, BC = EF, and angle B = angle E. A rigid motion moves B onto E and ray BA onto ray ED. Explain why A lands on D and C lands on F.
questions.correct_answer: A lands on D because AB = DE along the same ray. Because angle B = angle E, ray BC lands on ray EF (after a reflection if needed), and because BC = EF, C lands on F. So the triangles are congruent (SAS).

questions.set_title: Decide whether given conditions make one triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle
questions.section_title: Explain triangle congruence criteria with rigid motions
questions.question: Triangles PQR and STU have PQ = ST, QR = TU, and PR = SU. A rigid motion moves P onto S and Q onto T, with R and U on the same side of ST. Explain why R must land on U.
questions.correct_answer: R lands where a circle of radius PR around S meets a circle of radius QR around T on that side of ST. U is that same point (SU = PR and TU = QR), and there is only one such point, so R lands on U (SSS).

The rays from D and E at the equal angles cross at only one point, so C and F are the same point.

questions.set_title: Explain the relationship between the circumference and the area of a circle
questions.section_title: Grade 7 main question
questions.question: The circle with radius r is cut into equal wedges and rearranged as shown. Explain how this shows that the area of a circle is πr².
questions.required_method: A complete argument: the rearranged shape is close to a parallelogram (a rectangle with more wedges); its base is half the circumference, {1/2} × 2πr = πr; its height is the radius r; so its area is πr × r = πr², and the circle has the same area because it is made of the same wedges. Any equivalent wording is accepted.

questions.section_title: Use a simulation to decide whether a difference between treatments is significant
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: In an experiment, 40 similar plants were randomly assigned: 20 got a new plant food (Group A) and 20 got none (Group B). Group A grew a mean of 12 cm and Group B a mean of 9 cm. The data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect; a difference of 3 cm or more happened 2 times. Is there evidence that the plant food made a difference? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. With random assignment, a difference that large happened by chance only about 2% of the time, so the results give evidence of a treatment effect (but do not prove it).

questions.question: In the same kind of randomized experiment (plants randomly assigned to plant food or none), the data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect. A difference of 3 cm or more happened 40 times. What does this suggest about the plant food?
questions.correct_answer: The difference could easily be due to chance, so the experiment does not give evidence that the plant food made a difference.
